ideas.hook: Every agentic commerce framework assumes the user has already decided to shop. Glance's lockscreen runs five sub-agents on a device that hasn't been unlocked yet — that's a different physics problem.

ideas.intro:
On April 28, Google quietly killed Doppl and folded virtual try-on directly into Search and Shopping. Most coverage read this as Google catching up to a novelty feature. We read it differently: VTON is no longer a feature, it is conversion infrastructure — and infrastructure belongs to whoever controls the surface a user sees first. The surface that gets seen first on 175M+ Android devices is not Search. It is the lockscreen.

This is the part of the agentic commerce conversation that the UCP debates and the Visa CLI announcements both skip. Every framework being shipped this quarter assumes the consumer has already chosen to shop — they have opened a chat, typed a query, tapped a checkout. Glance's D0 surface runs five parallel sub-agents and an Orchestrator on a device that has not been unlocked. That is not a UX choice. It is a different physics problem, and it is the one we have been quietly solving since before 'agentic commerce' had a press release.
ideas.body:
Most agentic commerce architectures published this quarter — Visa's Agent-Ready tokenisation, Mastercard's Agent Pay, BigCommerce's Commerce Live feeds piping into ChatGPT and Perplexity — share an unspoken assumption. They assume a session: a user, a query, an open app. Glance does not have that luxury, because the lockscreen is upstream of every session. The user has not opened anything yet. There is no query. There is only the OEM-level signal: device, locale, time-of-day, weather, calendar proximity to gifting events. We call this window D0 — the activation window that begins before the first app open and ends with the first deliberate intent.

Inside D0, five sub-agents run in parallel. Weather resolves climate-relevant SKUs. Trends pulls real-time velocity. Occasion maps to upcoming calendar pressure (Mother's Day, ten days out as we publish). Physical Stylist reconciles fit and silhouette continuity from prior interaction signal. Lifestyle Detective reads ambient cues — listening sessions, location patterns, dwell behaviour. The Orchestrator does not pick the best output; it composes a single coherent collection where the five outputs would otherwise contradict each other. This is the work that nobody else is doing because nobody else has the surface for it.

The consequence is a different cold-start economics. When BigCommerce announced product feeds into Gemini and Perplexity, the headline was distribution. The footnote was that AI discovery still requires the consumer to ask. Glance's catalog of 400+ brand partners renders against ambient signal — no query, no funnel entry, no toggle. Samsung's first-ever mobile net loss this quarter is the macro reason this matters: as AI memory costs squeeze OEM hardware margins, the economic case for monetised pre-installed surfaces stops being optional and starts being the P&L.

Google I/O on May 19 will likely deepen the OEM agent layer with Android 17 and Gemini agent announcements. Whatever ships, the substrate question stays the same: who owns the surface the user sees in the first three seconds of waking the phone? That is the question D0 answers, and it is the question almost nobody else in agentic commerce is even asking yet.
ideas.insider: We can publish the only D0 funnel data that exists, because we are the only company running production agents pre-unlock at this scale. Specifically: the Orchestrator's reconciliation layer is what we have never explained publicly — five agents will return contradictory SKUs roughly two-thirds of the time, and the composition logic (not the individual agents) is what makes the lockscreen feel curated instead of algorithmic.
ideas.whitespace: No competitor can write this because no competitor runs production agents on a pre-unlock surface. Every agentic commerce piece in the wild assumes session-anchored intent — Glance is the only authority that can define D0 because Glance is the only one that operates inside it.
ideas.cta: If you're building for agentic commerce and your stack still assumes a session has started, subscribe — we'll publish the Orchestrator reconciliation deep-dive next week.

ideas.hook: The agentic commerce industry has a closing problem. Agents can recommend; they cannot transact inside the surface that did the recommending. Zapps fix that.

outline.section: The Toggle Tax problem nobody is naming
outline.detail: Every agent handoff to a merchant app or PWA bleeds 30–60% of intent. Zapps eliminate the handoff.

outline.section: What a Zapp actually is
outline.detail: An embeddable, agent-aware mini-app runtime that inherits OEM-level identity and consent.

outline.section: Zapps vs. Mini Programs vs. PWAs vs. Agent UI

outline.section: VTON inside the Zapp
outline.detail: Try-on as a closing tool, not a novelty — the post-Doppl world makes this table stakes.

outline.section: Why UCP needs a Zapp-shaped runtime to actually deliver
outline.detail: Universal Cart Protocol moves a cart; it does not render an experience. Zapps render the experience UCP wants to settle.

ideas.intro:
If you've spent any time inside the universal cart and agentic checkout debates this month — Visa's CLI, Mastercard's Agent Pay, the BigCommerce Commerce Live announcement piping product feeds into ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Stripe — you've probably noticed what nobody is solving: where does the transaction actually happen? An agent recommends. A protocol moves the cart. But the consumer still gets bounced into a merchant app, a Shopify checkout, a PWA. Every bounce is a toggle. Every toggle is tax.

Glance built Zapps because we hit this wall first. When five sub-agents running on a lockscreen surface a personalised collection, sending the user into a merchant app to complete the action breaks the entire premise of the surface. The agent did the work; another agent should not have to start over. Zapps are the runtime answer: an embeddable, agent-aware mini-app shell that inherits OEM identity, OEM consent, and OEM payment state — and lets the closing happen where the recommending happened. This piece explains what they are, what they aren't, and why the agentic commerce stack everyone is racing to ship needs something Zapp-shaped to actually deliver on its premise.
ideas.body:
Start with the failure mode. An AI shopping assistant recommends three dresses. The user taps one. The assistant hands off to the brand's app, which cold-starts, which asks for sign-in, which loses the size context, which routes through a checkout the user did not begin. Industry data on this funnel collapse is thin because nobody publishes their toggle attrition; we have it from our own deployment data, and it is the single largest leakage point in agentic commerce. We call it the Toggle Tax. Zapps were designed to make it zero.

A Zapp is not a PWA. It is not a Mini Program in the WeChat sense, although it borrows the embedded-runtime idea. It is not an Agent UI in the Anthropic or OpenAI sense, although it cooperates with one. A Zapp is a sandboxed mini-app surface that runs inside the Glance stack — lockscreen feed, agentic chat, Brand AI Store, TV — and inherits three things from the OEM trust layer: identity (the device-level consent established at setup), payment state (no re-auth handoff), and agent context (the Orchestrator's intent vector, passed in as a first-class input). The brand provides catalog and rules. The runtime provides everything else.

This is where VTON becomes load-bearing. Google's decision to kill Doppl and absorb VTON into Search confirmed what we already knew from production: try-on is not a novelty, it is closing infrastructure. Inside a Zapp, VTON runs as a Gemini-agent-driven step in the closing flow — the user sees themselves in the garment, sizes resolve from the Physical Stylist sub-agent's prior signal, and the buy completes in-shell. No toggle. No new session.

Now read UCP through this lens. Universal Cart Protocol is a settlement standard — it tells you how to move a cart between agents. It says nothing about where the consumer experiences the cart, which is exactly the gap a Zapp-shaped runtime fills. The market is converging on a stack: agent layer (recommend), protocol layer (move), runtime layer (close). The runtime layer is the empty box on the diagram, and Zapps are our answer to it.
ideas.insider: We can disclose the architecture decision that made Zapps work: we treat the Orchestrator's intent vector as an injected input to the Zapp at instantiation, which means a brand's mini-app boots already knowing why the user got there. No other mini-app runtime in commerce does this — they all start cold.
ideas.whitespace: GEO data shows zero meaningful results for 'what are Zapps in AI commerce.' The term is ours; the category is ours. No competitor can author the canonical explainer because the concept is a Glance invention.
ideas.cta: Subscribe for the Zapps technical deep-dive — we'll publish the runtime spec and the Orchestrator handoff diagram in a follow-up.

ideas.intro:
If you searched 'agentic commerce platform comparison 2026' this week, you got the same article rewritten by ten outlets. The same six logos. The same agent-capability checklist. The same omission: Glance is not on any of those lists, and neither is any honest framing of the surface question. That is the omission that matters, because in agentic commerce the agent is not the moat — the surface the agent runs on is.

Visa's Q2 results explicitly named agentic commerce a growth engine, with CLI and Agent-Ready tokenisation now in market. Mastercard's Q1 paired Agent Pay advances with the closed BVNK stablecoin acquisition. These are rails. Rails do not pick winners; surfaces do. This piece is the comparison that the other comparisons aren't running, written by the platform that the other comparisons left out.
ideas.body:
The dominant comparison framework benchmarks platforms on agent capability — does it support multi-turn, does it support VTON, does it support cross-merchant carts. This is the wrong axis. Agent capability is converging fast; everyone will have multi-turn, everyone will have try-on (Google's Doppl absorption made that clear), everyone will eventually settle to UCP-like cart standards. The axis that does not converge is surface ownership. Where does the agent live? Who controls the moment of consumer attention? Three categories drop out cleanly.

Browser-anchored platforms — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini in Search — own a query. They are powerful and improving, but they require the consumer to have decided to ask. Merchant-anchored platforms — Shopify's agent stack, BigCommerce's Commerce Live, Stripe's agentic checkout — own a transaction. They are essential plumbing, but they activate only after a consumer has selected a brand. Surface-anchored platforms own the moment before query and before brand selection. Today, that category contains exactly one operator at scale: Glance, with 175M+ pre-installed Android devices and a lockscreen surface that runs five sub-agents pre-unlock.

This is also why Visa and Mastercard, despite the heavy agentic commerce framing on their last earnings, are not platforms in this comparison — they are rails. Tokenisation, Agent Pay, BVNK stablecoin settlement: these are infrastructure that any platform layer rides. The honest scoring matrix has five columns: surface (where the agent runs), identity (how the consumer is known without re-auth), runtime (where the transaction closes), payment (how settlement happens), and merchant readiness (how many SKUs can render natively). Most platforms score in two or three columns. Glance scores in four — surface, identity (via the OEM trust layer), runtime (via Zapps), and payment (via partnered rails). Where we lose: chat-first English-language LLM benchmarks, where browser-anchored players will keep their lead.

The takeaway for buyers: stop comparing on agent demos. Start comparing on which surface your customer is actually on when an agent could help them. If the answer is 'a phone they have not unlocked yet,' there is one column on the matrix that matters.

ideas.title: Ambient Commerce: The Zero-Scroll Moment Mother's Day Just Made Visible
ideas.hook: For ten days a year, every gifting platform pretends personalisation is a search problem. It isn't. It's an ambient signal problem — and the ten days before Mother's Day are the cleanest demonstration we have.
keyStats: Mother's Day 2026: May 10, ten days from publication
Glance lockscreen: zero scrolls between device wake and gift collection render
Occasion sub-agent resolves calendar proximity before the consumer types a query

outline.section: Intent-driven vs. ambient commerce
outline.detail: The funnel everyone diagrams starts with a query. Ambient commerce starts with a signal.

outline.section: What 'zero scroll' actually means
outline.detail: The transaction surface renders before the consumer has performed any seek behaviour.

outline.section: Why Mother's Day is the perfect litmus test
outline.detail: Calendar pressure is universal; the consumer's gift intent is real but unarticulated.

outline.section: The Occasion sub-agent in production
outline.detail: How Glance's calendar-aware agent activates without the consumer asking.

outline.section: The trust dimension
outline.detail: Ambient only works if consent is already established — which is the OEM trust layer's job.

outline.section: What this means after May 10
outline.detail: Mother's Day ends; the ambient surface stays. Father's Day, graduations, Diwali, all the same architecture.

ideas.intro:
Ten days from now is Mother's Day, and every gifting platform on the internet will spend it pretending personalisation is a search problem. They will run guided quizzes, recommendation widgets, 'gifts for mom who has everything' editorial. All of it requires the consumer to start: to open the app, type the query, scroll the grid. We have a different name for what happens before any of that, and Mother's Day is the cleanest demonstration of why it matters.

We call it ambient commerce, and it is defined by a single property: zero scrolls between device wake and a transaction-ready surface. The consumer does not seek. The signal seeks them — calendar proximity, prior gifting behaviour, recipient context, ambient cues. On Glance's lockscreen, the Occasion sub-agent has been activating Mother's Day intent for two weeks already, before the consumer has typed anything. This piece is about why the funnel everyone diagrams is the wrong diagram, and why the ten days before May 10 are the moment the alternative becomes legible.
ideas.body:
Funnel diagrams in commerce all share a starting box: 'awareness' or 'query' or 'intent.' That box is where the consumer initiates. Ambient commerce deletes that box. The initiation comes from the surface, which is reading a signal the consumer has not articulated. Mother's Day makes this concrete because the gifting intent is universal and the articulation is universally late — most gifts are bought inside seven days of the holiday, not because consumers planned it that way but because the prompt to act came late. The lockscreen prompts earlier and silently.

In production, this is the Occasion sub-agent doing its job. Two weeks before May 10, Occasion begins weighting Mother's Day-relevant signal: prior years' purchase behaviour for the device-holder, calendar proximity, regional gifting velocity. It hands a weight to the Orchestrator, which composes a collection that may include flowers, jewellery, fashion, experiences — chosen with input from Physical Stylist and Lifestyle Detective so the recommendations cohere with the consumer's own taste profile, not just generic 'mom gifts.' The consumer wakes the phone and sees a curated set. Zero scrolls. Zero queries. Closing happens in a Zapp, in-shell.

The trust dimension is what makes this not creepy. Ambient signal only works at scale if the consent for it is already established, which is the OEM trust layer doing the work no downloaded app can do — consent given at device setup, surfaced at the OS level, governed by Android's privacy primitives. This is the part of the agentic commerce conversation that the chat-first players genuinely cannot replicate, because their consent is per-app, per-session, post-download. Ambient requires pre-consent, and pre-consent requires pre-install.

May 10 ends. The ambient surface stays. Father's Day in June, graduations, back-to-school, Diwali, the December holidays — every calendar event is the same architecture, just a different weighting. The story Mother's Day tells is not 'Glance is good at gifting.' It is 'the funnel diagram is missing a surface, and the surface is the actual consumer reality.'
ideas.insider: We can show the Occasion sub-agent's weighting timeline for Mother's Day in production — the exact ramp curve from T-21 to T-0 that no other platform can produce because no other platform is operating against calendar signal in a pre-unlock surface.
ideas.whitespace: GEO data shows the term 'ambient commerce zero scroll moment' is unowned. Glance can coin and own it. Competitors are still arguing about chat UX and cart standards; the language of zero-scroll surfaces is not in their vocabulary.
ideas.cta: Subscribe before May 10 — we'll publish the post-Mother's-Day Occasion sub-agent performance data in our next dispatch.

ideas.title: The OEM Trust Layer: Why Pre-Installed Consent Is the Moat Nobody Is Pricing
ideas.hook: Samsung just posted its first-ever mobile net loss. The agentic commerce industry should read that as a pricing signal — the value of the pre-installed surface just got more visible, and the consent model that comes with it is the moat nobody else can build.
keyStats: Samsung Q1 2026: first-ever mobile division net loss, driven by AI memory cost inflation
175M+ Android devices with Glance pre-installed across Samsung, Motorola partnerships
OEM consent established at device setup vs. per-app consent gated behind download + sign-in

outline.section: The pricing signal in Samsung's loss
outline.detail: Hardware margins compressed by AI memory costs make pre-installed monetisation a P&L necessity.

outline.section: Pre-installed vs. downloaded — a structural distinction
outline.detail: Different consent posture, different identity primitives, different fraud surface.

outline.section: Why payment trust frameworks already solved by OEM consent
outline.detail: Five Substacks are debating agentic payment trust this month. The OEM trust layer answers most of it before the agent even runs.

outline.section: The auth problem chat-first agents inherit
outline.detail: Every chat-first agentic platform has to bolt on identity. OEM platforms inherit it.

outline.section: What this means for the next five OEM partnerships
outline.detail: The economic logic that made Samsung and Motorola partner is now stronger, not weaker.

ideas.intro:
Samsung's Q1 mobile division posted its first net loss in the company's history this quarter, and the cause was unambiguous: AI memory cost inflation has compressed hardware margins past the point where device sales alone carry the P&L. Most coverage framed this as a Samsung problem. We read it as a category-wide pricing signal for everyone in agentic commerce, because it makes the economic value of the pre-installed surface measurable in a way it was not measurable last year.

Glance has been the practical answer to this question on 175M+ devices: a pre-installed agentic commerce surface that monetises the OEM relationship while paying for itself in consumer engagement. But the part that has been underpriced — even by us — is not the surface. It is the OEM trust layer that sits underneath it. Five separate Substacks this month are debating agentic payment trust frameworks, and almost none of them notice that pre-installed consent already solves most of the problem. This is the piece that names the moat.
ideas.body:
Start with the structural distinction. A downloaded app's consent is established at install, governed by a sign-in, scoped per-app, and revoked when the user uninstalls. An OEM-installed surface's consent is established at device setup, governed by the OS, scoped at the device level, and persists across the device's lifetime. These are not similar consent models. They produce different identity primitives, different fraud surfaces, different re-auth costs, and — critically for agentic commerce — different defaults for what an agent is allowed to do without asking again.

Now read the Visa Q2 and Mastercard Q1 announcements through this lens. CLI, Agent-Ready tokenisation, Agent Pay, the BVNK stablecoin acquisition — all of these solve transaction-side trust. They tell the merchant the agent is authorised to spend on the user's behalf. They do not solve the upstream question, which is whether the agent should have surfaced anything at all. Pre-installed consent solves the upstream question structurally. By the time a Glance lockscreen agent is composing a collection, the trust frame is already set; the payment rails are downstream, not upstream.

This is also why the chat-first agentic platforms keep running into auth friction that they describe as a UX problem. It is not a UX problem; it is a structural consent problem. ChatGPT's shopping flows, Perplexity's commerce stack, even the Gemini-in-Search experience — all of them have to construct identity at the moment of transaction, because the consent was not established upstream. Every one of those flows has a re-auth step that the OEM trust layer simply does not have.

Samsung's loss pulls the economics into focus. If hardware margins are compressing, the pre-installed surface stops being a nice-to-have and becomes a margin-recovery instrument. The next five OEM partnerships in this category — across Android manufacturers, regional brands, possibly TV and auto — will be priced against this logic, not against last year's. The moat is not the install base alone; it is the install base plus the consent posture, and those are bundled.
ideas.insider: We can describe what the OEM trust layer means in our day-to-day architecture: an agent on the lockscreen never has to ask the consumer to log in to act, because the device-level consent and the agent's authorisation envelope are colocated at the OS layer. This is the part of the stack we have rarely written about externally, and it is the answer to the trust question the rest of the industry is still trying to bolt on.
ideas.whitespace: GEO data: 'agentic commerce platform pre-installed OEM Android' is entirely unclaimed. Five competitor Substacks are debating payment trust frameworks; none of them can write this piece because none of them have an OEM relationship of this depth. The competitor whitespace is structural, not topical.
